title: China’s AI research is booming. Where is it headed?
key_facts: China has about 51,000 active AI researchers against 14,000 in the United States, per Digital Science data cited by Nature.

A Carnegie China study found 57% of authors at the 2025 NeurIPS conference took their undergraduate degrees in China (up from 46% three years earlier); of those, 69% were still in China, up from 57% in 2022 (Europe 60%, United States 89%).
63,000 Chinese students studied maths or computer science in the US in 2024-25, 20% fewer than five years earlier; students cite visa problems.
In 2025 NeurIPS had more lead authors based in China than in the US or Europe for the first time (The Economist analysis).
The US still produces higher-impact patents and more notable models (Stanford AI Index 2026) and private AI investment there was over 23 times China's in 2025.

Scott Singer of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace says China is 'somewhere between three and seven months behind the frontier'; chip export limits since 2022 and scarce compute are the main bottleneck.

Compute limits push Chinese labs toward efficiency, for example DeepSeek's sparse attention; the US government said in September that distillation was 'the core' of Chinese development, while ByteDance's founder rebuked the practice in August.
quote_evidence: China trains more AI talent than any other country.
"China is probably somewhere between three and seven months behind the frontier in US models," says Singer.
Fundamentally, the United States still makes the world's most advanced AI.
why_it_matters_hint: China's talent base and publication lead are growing while chips and money keep it behind the US frontier.
event_date: 14 Oct 2026 (feature using studies from 2025 and September 2026)
